knowledge_units.context_summary: The paper argues that in the far future of the ΛCDM universe, evidence for expansion, the CMB, and primordial nucleosynthesis will vanish, making the universe appear static to local observers. It reviews the historical de Sitter model, noting its static coordinate representation and its actual eternal expansion driven by a cosmological constant. Current observational data supports a flat universe composed of approximately 30% matter and 70% dark energy.

This transition implies that future observers within bound systems will perceive a static universe, losing access to evidence of the Big Bang and cosmic expansion.

knowledge_units.context_summary: Future observers in a static 'island universe' will be unable to detect dark energy or the Hubble expansion due to the dominance of vacuum energy and the redshifting of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) beyond the horizon. The CMB will become unobservable as its peak wavelength redshifts below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium, a process occurring well before the end of the longest-lived main sequence stars.

knowledge_units.context_summary: Future observers in a static island universe will be unable to detect CMB fluctuations or primordial elemental abundances due to redshifting and stellar processing. General relativity remains consistent with a static, empty universe outside local gravitational systems, preventing the inference of a Big Bang singularity. The current deuterium abundance evidence from quasar absorption systems will become inaccessible as these sources exit the horizon.

The current epoch is unique because it allows for the observational verification of both cosmic expansion and dark energy, a capability that will be lost in the future.
